guideTitle: 6 Best Fruit Pickers for Oranges and Lemons in 2026
metaTitle: Best Fruit Pickers for Oranges and Lemons
metaDescription: Six fruit pickers suited to oranges, lemons and other citrus, from short compact poles to taller telescoping models, with advice on basket size and reach.
mainKeyword: best fruit pickers for oranges and lemons
introParagraphs: Citrus trees are generous and awkward in equal measure. A healthy orange or lemon tree carries fruit from knee height to well above your head, the best fruit often sits in the crown, and the fruit itself is firm, round and surprisingly heavy. Add the thorns on many lemon varieties and the sticky juice that follows a dropped fruit, and it is easy to see why a long-handled picker is more than a convenience for anyone who no longer wants to climb a ladder. A picker also lets you take only what is ripe, instead of shaking the branch and bringing down green fruit along with it.

The six picks here are chosen for citrus in particular. The DonSail pomelo pole carries a roomy metal basket described for oranges and apples, the Walensee 5.5FT and BlumeTrec 6.5FT are compact poles for lower branches, and the ALongwujin has rubber-capped claws for gentle grabbing. The Draupnir 11.5FT trades a rigid basket for a cloth bag, and the SKGPOLE aluminum telescoping pole reaches into taller trees. Between them they cover trees from a patio pot to a mature backyard giant.

We evaluated each pick from its listing specs and what buyers say about everyday use, so sizes and materials are as the makers state them. Before you buy, remember the two rules that matter most with citrus: pick the shortest pole that reaches, and keep any metal pole well clear of overhead power lines. Think about where the fruit lands as well: a patch of grass or a cloth sheet beneath the tree saves any that miss the basket. Citrus can hang on the tree for weeks after ripening, so there is no need to rush a harvest in poor weather. Taste a fruit before you commit to picking the whole tree, since color is not always a reliable guide to sweetness.

products.name: DonSail Pomelo Fruit Picker Pole, 35 to 95 Inch
specs: Metal twist-on basket about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches
Listed for apple, pear, orange and avocado
products.description:
The DonSail pomelo pole is the one that most closely matches how oranges grow and weigh. It adjusts in sections from 35 to 95 inches, and the metal twist-on basket measures about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches, deep enough to hold an orange or two without letting them roll out. The listing names oranges, apples, pears and avocados among suitable fruit, and the shaft is 1 inch stainless steel.

The name nods at pomelo, the largest citrus, and that size tells you the basket is built for bulky fruit. For a standard navel or Valencia orange, there is room to spare, and a lemon sits easily in the cup. A deep basket is the difference between a calm harvest and one where every second fruit bounces off your shoes.

The tradeoff is that a long steel shaft with a loaded basket is tip-heavy, so shorten the pole between picks. Compared with the Walensee 5.5FT, the DonSail reaches almost twice as high. Compared with the SKGPOLE, it has a bigger basket but far less height. Its 95 inches beats the Walensee 5.5FT's 65 by 30 inches, which is enough for a standard backyard orange tree. Set the length so your elbows stay below shoulder height, and lower the pole each time before you empty the basket into a crate. Rinse the head after a session with a hose, since citrus juice dries into a sticky film that attracts ants. Because it is a sectional pole, you can leave the top sections off for a low branch and add them back for the crown without any tools.
products.bestFor: Backyard orange and grapefruit trees up to about eight feet of reach.

products.name: Walensee 5.5FT Fruit Picker with Basket
products.description:
The Walensee 5.5FT is a compact fruit picker that adjusts from 35 to 65 inches. Its basket has a cushioned foam pad that absorbs impact when fruit drops, helping reduce bruising, and the shaft is reinforced stainless steel.

For citrus it suits a dwarf lemon or a potted orange, where the fruit hangs within easy reach. The pad protects thin-skinned fruit such as Meyer lemons and tangerines, which show marks quickly. A shorter pole is easy to aim and light on the shoulders, so you can work for a long session without tiring.

The cost of that compactness is reach, and 65 inches will not touch the top of a mature tree. Compared with the BlumeTrec 6.5FT, it is a little shorter but offers a similar foam cushion. It pairs naturally with a taller pole in a garden that mixes sizes, so the compact one handles the lower fruit while the long one tackles the crown. The 12 inches of reach it gives up to the BlumeTrec 6.5FT is the whole price of a pole that stays light on the shoulders.
products.bestFor: Dwarf and potted citrus where the fruit hangs at head height.

products.name: BlumeTrec 6.5FT Fruit Picker with Basket
specs: Thick foam pad at basket bottom
products.description:
The BlumeTrec 6.5FT builds a pole from 16 inch stainless steel sections, from 35 to 77 inches long. A thick foam pad at the base of the basket gives picked fruit a soft landing, according to the listing.

Why it fits citrus: the section lengths let you tune the pole to the exact branch. A lemon cluster at 70 inches wants a different length than one at 50, and with 16 inch steps you can set it without a lock. The foam also protects lemons, which can scratch and show marks on the rind.

Compared with the DonSail pomelo pole, the BlumeTrec reaches less but handles more easily. Compared with the Walensee 5.5FT, it adds twelve inches of reach. It is a good middle choice for a typical backyard lemon tree. To use it well, stand close to the trunk and slide the cup beneath a ripe lemon before giving a slow quarter turn. Lemon clusters often release two at a time, so keep the cup steady until both have dropped in.
products.bestFor: Backyard lemon trees where you want exact length control.
cons: Sections must be joined by hand
Not tall enough for mature trees

products.name: ALongwujin Fruit Picker Pole, 27 to 75 Inch
products.description:
The ALongwujin has a metal basket with rubber-capped claws, and its pole adjusts from 27 to 75 inches with interchangeable sections. The listing says it fits avocados, mangoes, apples, oranges and pears.

Rubber-capped claws matter for citrus because they hold the fruit without piercing the rind. A scratched orange shows brown marks quickly and can start to rot in the bowl. The claws grip and twist, which is the motion that releases citrus from its stem.

It shares the 75 inch ceiling of the BlumeTrec but offers a different grip style. Its rigid claw head is the opposite of the Draupnir's soft cloth bag, which is the real choice between gripping a fruit and catching it. Compared with the Draupnir, it is shorter but has a rigid head. Slide the claws around the shoulder of the fruit rather than the top, which spreads the pressure and keeps the rind clean. For fruit with leaves tucked around it, a gentle wiggle frees the stem without tearing the foliage.
products.bestFor: A gentle grip on oranges and lemons at moderate height.

products.name: Draupnir 11.5FT Fruit Picker Pole with Cloth Bag
products.description:
The Draupnir 11.5FT is a stainless steel extension pole made of eight parts with a cloth fruit picker bag. The listing says the cloth bag gently catches fruit, and the rods can withstand general wear and tear.

A bag works differently from a basket: instead of a rigid cup, fruit lands in a soft pouch. That helps with lemons and oranges that you do not want to scratch or dent. It also folds flat for storage. The pole's eight parts connect to the length you want.

A cloth bag can sag under a lot of fruit and does not hold a shape the way metal does, so you will need to empty it often. Compared with the DonSail, the Draupnir has more reach but a less structured catch. At about 11.5 feet it out-reaches the Walensee 5.5FT by more than six feet, a gap that decides which lemons you can pick from the ground. Because the bag is soft, tip the pole toward you after each pick and let the fruit settle at the bottom. After use, shake out any leaves and let the bag dry flat before folding it away.
products.bestFor: Soft handling on medium-height trees with lots of lemons.
pros: Cloth bag is gentle on rind
cons: Less structure than a metal basket

products.name: SKGPOLE 26FT Reach Fruit Picker
specs: 5.5 inch metal basket with thick foam
products.description:
The SKGPOLE is for citrus trees that tower over you. Its aluminum telescoping pole runs from 5 to 20 feet with a maker-stated reach of up to 26 feet. The metal basket is 5.5 inches across with an ultra thick foam pad, and the thread is 3/4 inch American standard.

Mature oranges and lemons can grow ten feet or more, with the best fruit at the top. A tall aluminum pole gets there without a ladder, and the foam pad cushions a long fall. The basket is smaller than the DonSail's, so it suits lemons, limes and small oranges better than grapefruit.

Aluminum conducts electricity, and a pole this tall can touch wires before you notice. Compared with the Draupnir, the SKGPOLE reaches much higher. Use it only when the tree demands it. Its 5.5 inch cup against the DonSail's 9 by 5.5 inch head means large navel oranges are a tight fit, so lemons and limes are the better match. Retract the pole fully each time you move to the next branch, and never carry it extended. Owners with a tall, older tree can pair it with a ladder-free workflow by picking the lower half from the ground and leaving the top for a visit from a professional.
products.bestFor: Mature citrus trees with fruit well above head height.
pros: Reach up to 26 feet by the maker's claim

buyingCriteria.explanation: Oranges roll, so a deep cup matters. The DonSail pomelo basket measures about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches, while the SKGPOLE is 5.5 inches across. A shallow basket lets a round fruit bounce out. Match the basket to the biggest fruit you grow. For a tree with fruit at several heights, set the basket to the lowest fruit first and work upward, so the pole stays shorter for longer.

Citrus marks easily. The Walensee and BlumeTrec use foam pads, the ALongwujin has rubber-capped claws, and the Draupnir uses a cloth bag. A scratched rind can start to rot sooner. Choose padding if you plan to store fruit. If you plan to store oranges for a few weeks, protect the rind with extra care, because tiny abrasions become soft spots.

A dwarf lemon needs about 65 inches, a typical backyard tree about 95 inches, and a mature tree more than ten feet. The Walensee reaches 65 inches, the DonSail 95 inches, the Draupnir about 11.5 feet and the SKGPOLE up to 26 feet by the maker's claim. Do not buy more pole than you need. A good rule is to measure the highest fruit you want and add a foot for the basket and your own reach.

Citrus is heavy, so a loaded basket adds leverage. Aluminum poles like the SKGPOLE are lighter at the tip, while steel poles feel stiffer. Test the weight with a few fruit in the basket if you can. Practice with a few fruit on the ground to feel how the weight affects balance before you go up to the tree.

Many lemon trees have thorns, and a long pole keeps your hands and arms away from them. A pole of 65 inches or more gives you a safe distance. Wear gloves and long sleeves anyway. The 65 inch Walensee leaves your hands closest to the branches, so for a thorny lemon the BlumeTrec at 77 inches or the DonSail at 95 gives more distance.

Metal poles conduct electricity and can cause serious injury near overhead wires. Look up before extending any pole. Keep well clear, especially in wet weather. Wet weather is when the 26 foot SKGPOLE and the 11.5 foot Draupnir are most hazardous, since they reach furthest toward wires.

howWeEvaluated.title: Citrus suitability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for listings that mention oranges or similar fruit. The DonSail pomelo and ALongwujin name oranges explicitly. We favored deeper baskets and rind-friendly grips. A deep cup that stops oranges rolling out counted for more than a bigger reach figure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fruit protection
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared padding. The Walensee and BlumeTrec have foam pads, the ALongwujin has rubber claws, and the Draupnir has a cloth bag. Foam pads were a decisive factor for thin-skinned fruit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach range
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched reach to tree sizes, from 65 inches on the Walensee to 26 feet on the SKGPOLE. Reach figures are the makers' claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered steel versus aluminum and how a full load changes handling. Steel feels stiffer, and aluminum feels lighter.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted electrical risk for every metal pole, and treated safety guidance as part of the ranking. The SKGPOLE and Draupnir, which reach highest, were judged most strictly here.

faq.q: How do I pick oranges without bruising them?
faq.a: Lift the basket under the fruit and twist gently so the stem releases. Do not yank or drop the fruit. A foam pad helps. Pick when the fruit comes away with a light twist. Citrus keeps best when it is picked dry, so wait until the morning dew has gone.

A basket about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches, like the DonSail, holds oranges comfortably. A 5.5 inch diameter basket is fine for lemons. Larger citrus needs a deeper cup. Match the cup to the largest orange you expect. If the basket opening is narrow, tangerines and limes will go in more easily than grapefruit.

faq.q: Is a cloth bag better than a basket?
faq.a: A cloth bag is gentler but sags. A basket holds shape and weight. Many gardeners use one of each. In this guide the Draupnir is the cloth-bag pole, while the rest use baskets or claws. A bag also takes up less room in a drawer, which is handy for a small household.

faq.q: How do I deal with thorns?
faq.a: Use a pole long enough to keep your arms back. Wear gloves and long sleeves. Pick from outside in. The 65 inch Walensee is the pole that keeps your hands closest to thorns, so choose the BlumeTrec or DonSail for a thorny lemon.

faq.q: Are these safe near power lines?
faq.a: No. Metal poles conduct electricity. Look up before extending and keep well clear. Call the utility if a tree touches a wire. The SKGPOLE and Draupnir, the two tallest poles here, need this check most. Avoid working near lines during a storm, when the ground and the pole are both wet.

faq.q: Can I pick lemons and oranges with the same pole?
faq.a: Yes, if the basket is deep enough for the larger fruit. The DonSail pomelo pole handles both. Choose a taller pole for tall trees. Choose by the highest fruit you want. A pole that is too large for lemons is only a little harder to use, but a basket that is too small for oranges is a constant frustration.
